dialogues.speaker: LCROSS
dialogues.text: Four minutes. That's all the time I had after Centaur slammed into Cabeus and before I crashed down right after it. Time flew by so fast, every passing second flooded with streams of data pouring in from my instruments.

dialogues.speaker: LCROSS
dialogues.text: I flew right through the impact dust cloud—a cloud that might look like a tiny puff of dust from Earth, but in the silence of the Moon, it felt like a secret door being forced open.

dialogues.speaker: LCROSS
dialogues.text: Signs of water, that was my mission. In science, water has a signature look that spectrometers can easily spot. When sunlight passes through water vapor, H2O molecules absorb light at specific wavelengths, especially in the near-infrared range.

dialogues.speaker: LCROSS
dialogues.text: My infrared spectrometer worked overtime, carving through the light coming from the dust plume. What I saw made those data transmissions pulse back to Earth with total urgency: a super distinct absorption signal. Water, and a whole lot of it.

dialogues.speaker: LCROSS
dialogues.text: And not just water vapor, either. Hidden in the data I gathered, my infrared camera picked up signs of ice crystals—water in solid form, frozen solid at sub-zero temperatures.

dialogues.speaker: LCROSS
dialogues.text: Scientists back on Earth, pulling in my data through the Deep Space Network, realized right away that what I was looking at wasn't just a tiny trace of moisture, but real, actual water deposits.

dialogues.speaker: LCROSS
dialogues.text: Months after the mission wrapped up, a team of scientists led by Anthony Colaprete analyzed the data and published the results in the journal Science in October 2010. The numbers they dropped shook the scientific world: roughly 155 kilograms, or 342 pounds, of water vapor and water ice were blasted out of the crater from the Centaur's impact.

dialogues.speaker: LCROSS
dialogues.text: From those calculations, they estimated that about 5.6 percent of the material mass inside Cabeus Crater was water ice. That number was way higher than anyone had guessed. It was like finding out that hidden behind the crater's eternal shadows, the Moon was actually hoarding a massive store of ice.

dialogues.speaker: LCROSS
dialogues.text: But water wasn't the only thing uncovered. The dust cloud I ran into turned out to be packed with other mind-blowing compounds. There was hydroxyl, a close relative of water molecules. There was carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, methane, ammonia, and even a tiny bit of hydrogen cyanide.

dialogues.speaker: LCROSS
dialogues.text: We even found silver and mercury—metals no one expected to find floating around on the Moon. For the scientists, that mix was like reading a geological diary billions of years in the making: footprints of comet impacts, blasts of solar wind, and slow-motion chemical processes happening at temperatures close to absolute zero.

dialogues.speaker: LCROSS
dialogues.text: Turns out the Moon isn't a completely dead world after all. It has an ultra-slow water cycle and chemical reactions still ticking away, even down in the dark.

dialogues.speaker: LCROSS
dialogues.text: After recording, measuring, and beaming back all the data, the Moon's gravity pulled me down. At 11:35 UTC, I slammed into Cabeus Crater. My job was done. The secrets of Cabeus were finally out.
